issues.description: Table 4 and the accompanying text report contradictory Bayes Factors. The text states 'Non-illusory error rates increased from the short to the long delay (BFincl = 190 for Memory Delay)' and that 'only Memory Delay was a relevant factor,' but Table 4 shows BFincl = 0.064 for Memory Delay (evidence AGAINST inclusion) and BFincl = 39110.895 for Target Type (strong evidence FOR inclusion). These values are directly contradictory; either the table labels are swapped, or the text is incorrect. This raises serious concerns about the accuracy of reported results.
issues.quote: For other, non-illusory errors only Memory Delay was a relevant factor (BFm = 42, see Appendix 1 for a full model comparison and Table 4 for an overview of BFincl for each model component). Non-illusory error rates increased from the short to the long delay (BFincl = 190 for Memory Delay) but this increase was the same for pseudo- and real letter targets

issues.description: In Experiment 1, 40 participants passed training, and the text states '23 participants (5 participants were excluded)' were included. However, 40 minus 5 equals 35, not 23. Either 17 participants were excluded (not 5), or the final sample size is wrong. The remaining 12 participants are unaccounted for, making it impossible to evaluate the integrity of the sample.
issues.quote: Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence critical trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) were excluded from the analysis resulted in an inclusion of 23 participants (5 participants were excluded) when the results were averaged across the set size conditions.

issues.description: In all experiments, the response display contains the mirrored counterpart of the target. At longer delays, when the memory trace is weaker, seeing the real letter among the response options could overwrite or bias retrieval of the weaker pseudo-letter memory trace. This means the increase in 'illusions' over time could reflect retrieval interference from the response display rather than a transformation of the stored memory representation. This alternative explanation is not addressed and fundamentally undermines the key claim that memory traces are being reshaped prior to retrieval.
issues.quote: The response screen consisted of 6 letters: the target letter (with the same orientation as in the memory display, or mirror reversed), two other randomly selected letters from the memory display, and 3 letters that did not appear in the memory display.

issues.description: The authors dismiss response bias as an explanation but provide no quantitative evidence against it. Participants may preferentially select familiar real letters from the response display not because they 'remember' seeing them, but because familiar items feel more fluent and thus elicit higher confidence. This perceptual fluency effect would produce exactly the observed pattern: more pseudo-to-real than real-to-pseudo errors, especially at high confidence, and more so when memory is weak (longer delays). High confidence does not necessarily index a genuine memory trace—it could reflect metacognitive bias toward familiar stimuli.
issues.quote: Yet another reason why illusory reports arise could be a response bias: Participant might just be more inclined to select real letters instead of pseudo-letters, since real letters are a well-known category. However, this is unlikely because the pattern of responses across conditions is consistent with memory-driven processes rather than response bias.

issues.description: Excluding participants with fewer than 10 high-confidence trials per cell, and then analyzing only high-confidence trials, creates a double selection bias. First, participants who are generally more confident (and may systematically differ in strategy or ability) are preferentially retained. Second, within retained participants, only confident trials are analyzed, which may not be representative. If confidence is itself related to the tendency to select familiar stimuli (real letters), this filtering procedure could artifactually inflate the apparent rate of pseudo-to-real illusions.
issues.quote: Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence critical trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) were excluded from the analysis

issues.description: Experiment 2 excludes 92 out of 290 participants (31.7%) based on insufficient high-confidence trials. Excluded participants had dramatically lower confidence rates (15.7% vs. 49.2%). This massive, non-random exclusion means the results only generalize to a subpopulation of highly confident responders. The characteristics of excluded participants may differ systematically, introducing survivorship bias.
issues.quote: Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) resulted in an inclusion of 198 participants (92 participants were excluded)

issues.description: The central argument that increasing errors over time proves memory-based (not perceptual) illusions has an important gap. An alternative explanation is that at shorter delays, a stronger memory trace can resist the biasing influence of the response display or retrieval processes, while at longer delays the weaker trace is more susceptible to bias at the point of retrieval/response selection. This means the temporal increase could reflect retrieval-stage bias interacting with trace strength, rather than a progressive transformation of the stored representation. The authors' logic requires that the illusion exists in the memory trace prior to seeing the response display, but this is not demonstrated.
issues.quote: If the illusions are simply the result of misperceptions, their frequency of occurrence should remain the same over the time-course of STM – since in all cases initial perceptual inference has been completed.

issues.description: Experiment 1 uses a 2-point confidence scale (1=guess, 2=certain), while Experiments 2-4 use a 4-point scale (1=guess, 4=certainty). The definition of 'high confidence' therefore differs across experiments. This inconsistency makes cross-experiment comparisons problematic and means the 'high confidence' filter selects different types of responses in different experiments. No justification is given for the change, and no analysis explores its impact.
issues.quote: After selecting the target letter, participants indicated their confidence by clicking on one of two boxes (from 1-2, 1 = guess, 2 = certain).

issues.description: In the Experiment 4 results section, the text refers to 'Figure 5' for the error rates, but Figure 5 is labeled as depicting Experiment 3 data. The correct reference should be to Figure 6, which is the figure for Experiment 4.
issues.quote: Figure 5 shows the error rates for high confidence trials.

issues.description: The authors argue that Fuzzy Trace Theory (FTT) is inconsistent with their data because FTT predicts high similarity should facilitate false memories, and they observe abundant false memories with highly similar stimuli. But this is actually consistent with FTT, not inconsistent. The authors appear to have made a logical error. They may have intended to argue that FTT cannot explain the asymmetry (pseudo-to-real > real-to-pseudo), but the text as written contradicts itself.
issues.quote: However, FTT predicts that high similarity between a target and its mirrored counterpart should facilitate false memories. This is not consistent with the current data: The mirrored counterpart (the real letter) and the target (the pseudo-letter) are extremely similar, yet false memories are abundant.

issues.description: Experiment 4 was conducted online via Zoom with participants using their own laptops. This introduces uncontrolled variability in display timing, screen size, resolution, refresh rate, viewing distance, and environmental distractions—all factors critical for a visual memory task with 250ms stimulus presentations. No validation of timing accuracy on participants' hardware is reported, and no analyses examine whether variability in these factors affected results.
issues.quote: the data was collected in an online experiment, using Neurotask scripting. Participants that signed up to take part in the experiment were invited to join a Zoom meeting at a preset time. Here, each participant was placed in a Zoom break-out room, and given the link to the Neurotask experiment, which they then started on their own laptop.

issues.description: In Experiment 1, the probability of the target appearing in the response display and the probability of its mirrored counterpart appearing differ substantially between real-letter and pseudo-letter targets (83% vs. 50% for target present; 16% vs. 50% for mirrored counterpart present). This asymmetry means participants encounter real letters in the response display more frequently overall, which could itself generate familiarity-based response biases. Although the authors address this in Experiment 2, the results of Experiment 1 are still interpreted as supporting the hypotheses.
issues.quote: If the target was a pseudo-letter, then it appeared as a response option randomly on half of those trials while on the other half of pseudo-letter trials only the real counterpart was one of the response options. If the target was a real letter, then it appeared as a response option on a randomly selected 83% of the trials, while its mirror reversed (pseudo-letter) version appeared as a response option on the other 16% of the trials.

issues.description: Experiments 3 and 4 use sequential Bayesian testing with different BF thresholds (BF=6 for Experiment 3, BF=10 for Experiment 4). No justification is given for the different thresholds or for choosing these specific values. The choice of stopping rule can influence final sample sizes and the strength of evidence obtained, and the inconsistency weakens the methodological rigor.
issues.quote: once the outcome crossed a BF of 6, testing would stop

issues.description: The Bayes Factor interpretation guidelines presented are asymmetric: BF < 0.33 (reciprocal = ~3) is labeled 'strong evidence for the null,' while BF > 10 is labeled 'strong evidence for the alternative.' Under standard Jeffreys guidelines, these should correspond (BF < 0.1 matching BF > 10, or BF < 0.33 matching BF > 3). This asymmetry means the evidentiary standard for the null and alternative hypotheses differs, potentially biasing interpretation.
issues.quote: Bayes Factors were interpreted as follows: BF < 0.33: strong evidence for the null hypothesis. 0.33 - 1: substantial evidence for the null hypothesis. 1 – 3: anecdotal evidence for the alternative hypothesis, 3 – 10: substantial evidence for the alternative hypothesis, >10: strong evidence for the alternative hypothesis

issues.description: Experiments 1 and 2 do not report any formal power analysis or sample size justification. Experiment 1 ends with only 23 participants after exclusion (potentially fewer—the numbers are unclear). Experiment 2's sample size was determined by course enrollment rather than statistical considerations. Without power analyses, it is unclear whether these studies were adequately powered to detect the relevant interaction effects.
issues.quote: The number of participants was determined not by the experimenter but by student enrollment in the course, which explains the large increase in participants compared to Experiment 1.

issues.description: Participants received trial-by-trial feedback on accuracy in Experiments 1 and 2, and block-level feedback in Experiments 2-4. This feedback could itself shape participants' expectations and strategies throughout the experiment. For instance, receiving 'incorrect' feedback when reporting a pseudo-letter (because they selected the real counterpart) could increase awareness of pseudo-letters and alter response patterns over the course of the experiment, confounding the effects of interest.
issues.quote: They were instructed to select "none of these" if the target letter was not a response option. After selecting the target letter, participants indicated their confidence by clicking on one of two boxes

issues.subcategory: generalizability limited to one stimulus class
issues.description: All four experiments use only letters/pseudo-letters as stimuli. The authors make broad claims about STM illusions and predictive processing in memory, but the findings might be specific to the highly overlearned category of letters. No experiments test whether similar effects occur with other stimulus types (e.g., familiar vs. unfamiliar objects, faces, or other visual patterns), limiting the generalizability of the conclusions.
issues.quote: In conclusion, four experiments consistently show that illusory memories arise even when the visual stimulus has only been out of sight for very brief periods of time.

issues.subcategory: confound between set size and pseudo-letter number
issues.description: In Experiment 1, set size (6 vs. 8 letters) is confounded with the number/proportion of pseudo-letters. Set size 8 always had 2 pseudo-letters (25%), while set size 6 had either 1 or 2 pseudo-letters (17% or 33%). This means any effects attributed to set size could be driven by the different proportion of pseudo-letters, or vice versa.
issues.quote: When the memory display consisted of 8 letters, it contained 2 pseudo-letters. When it contained 6 letters, it had a 50% chance of containing 1 pseudo-letter and a 50% chance of containing 2 pseudo-letters.

issues.description: The manuscript does not clearly state the threshold for 'high confidence' across experiments. In Experiment 1 with a 2-point scale, presumably only '2' (certain) counts as high confidence. In Experiments 2-4 with a 4-point scale, it is never explicitly stated which rating(s) constitute 'high confidence' (3 and 4? Only 4?). This ambiguity makes the results difficult to evaluate and replicate.
issues.quote: Subsequently she indicated confidence in her judgment (1 = guess, 4 = certainty).

issues.description: In all experiments, an 'irrelevant' second letter display is presented, which also contains real and pseudo-letters. Participants are instructed to ignore it, but it could serve as a visual prime, biasing participants toward selecting real letters. Its effects on the pattern of illusions are not independently measured or controlled for. In Experiment 1, the timing of this second display varies across conditions, adding another confound.
issues.quote: To increase memory decay through task-irrelevant interference, a second display was included in each trial. This display consisted of randomly selected letters, unrelated to the memory display. Participants were instructed to ignore this second display.

issues.description: In Experiment 1, participants had to score >75% on a cued change-detection training task to be included. This selects for participants with above-average visual STM ability, potentially limiting generalizability. Moreover, this training procedure was only used in Experiment 1, creating a between-experiment difference in participant selection.
issues.quote: Participants could only participate in the actual experiment, if they scored higher than 75% correct (averaged across all trials) on the final 10 blocks of training.

issues.description: Throughout all four experiments, effect sizes are not reported for any of the statistical comparisons. Only Bayes Factors and percentages are given. Without standardized effect sizes (e.g., Cohen's d, eta-squared), it is difficult to evaluate the practical significance of the findings or to compare them with other studies in the literature.
issues.quote: The Bayesian repeated measures ANOVA showed that a model with main effects for Error Type, Target Type, and Memory Delay, and a Target Type * Error Type and Memory Delay * Error Type interaction had the best fit (BFm = 18

issues.description: The discussion claims that illusory memories can occur during WM and FM stages of STM, but this is not directly demonstrated. The experimental designs do not include validated manipulations that specifically isolate WM versus FM, and the authors acknowledge they do not test iconic memory. Yet they make broad claims about the pervasiveness of illusions across STM substages.
issues.quote: Our findings suggest that illusory memories can occur during the WM and FM stages of STM. Experiment 1 shows that when the memory cue is presented together with unrelated information, a trial-type most like a WM manipulation, illusory memories are highly prevalent.

issues.description: The sentence describing the exclusion criterion in Experiment 1 is grammatically broken and difficult to parse, which contributes to the confusion about how many participants were actually excluded and included.
issues.quote: Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence critical trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) were excluded from the analysis resulted in an inclusion of 23 participants (5 participants were excluded)

issues.description: In Experiment 2, follow-up ANOVAs are conducted separately for illusory and non-illusory errors after a significant three-way interaction. However, this decomposition strategy is not pre-registered or justified, and different decompositions (e.g., by target type or by memory delay) could yield different interpretive conclusions. The choice to separate by error type may have been guided by the data pattern.
issues.quote: Follow-up ANOVAs conducted separately for each error type showed that for illusory errors, the optimal model consisted of the factors Memory delay, Target type and the interaction between the two

issues.subcategory: Experiment 2 color cue manipulation underpowered for detection
issues.description: The color cue manipulation in Experiment 2 used a 25% vs. 60% pseudo-letter target probability. Participants reportedly did not notice the contingency (per questionnaire). Without awareness of the contingency, it is unsurprising that the manipulation had no effect. The null result is interpreted as evidence that transient expectations do not influence STM illusions, but it may simply reflect a failure of the manipulation rather than a genuine null effect.
issues.quote: Participants filled out a brief questionnaire in which they were invited to indicate what the experiment was about after the experiment. The relationship between the colour of the cue and the nature of the target was not mentioned in any of the responses.

issues.subcategory: incomplete reporting of excluded data patterns
issues.description: The manuscript does not report whether the pattern of results differs when excluded participants are included (e.g., analyzing all trials regardless of confidence, or using a less strict exclusion criterion). Given the high exclusion rates, it is important to verify that the key findings are not artifacts of the exclusion procedure.
issues.quote: Excluded participants had on average 26.2% high confidence trials over all conditions (range 3.6 – 47.7%, sd: 13.0).
